definition.simple: A slow, steady change over many years, like a path that keeps going uphill or downhill.
definition.scientific: The average rate of change over the analysis window, estimated as a straight-line slope.

definition.simple: The ups and downs that happen every year, like summer being warmer than winter.
definition.scientific: The mean annual cycle, estimated as each calendar month's long-term mean over the window.

definition.simple: How much a month was above or below what is normal for that month.
definition.scientific: Value minus that calendar month's climatological mean (the seasonal cycle removed).

definition.simple: How much the value changes in 10 years if the trend keeps going.
definition.scientific: Slope expressed in units per 10 years.

definition.simple: A change so big and steady that it is very unlikely to be just luck.
definition.scientific: Both persistence-aware tests reject the no-trend hypothesis at α = 0.05 (two-sided).

definition.simple: We can't tell yet. The normal ups and downs are bigger than the change. It does NOT mean nothing is changing.
definition.scientific: Insufficient evidence to reject the no-trend hypothesis; this is not evidence of no trend.

definition.simple: How easily pure luck could make a pattern like this. Small numbers mean luck is a poor explanation.
definition.scientific: Probability of a result at least this extreme if there were no trend. It is not the probability that the trend is real.

definition.simple: The span where the true change probably sits. A narrow range means we are more sure.
definition.scientific: Interval for Sen's slope from the (persistence-corrected) Mann–Kendall variance at the 95% level.

definition.simple: When one month partly remembers the month before, like wet soil staying wet. It makes patterns look stronger than they are.
definition.scientific: Correlation between consecutive detrended anomalies (r₁); used to reduce the effective sample size.

definition.simple: We compare every pair of months and take the middle value of all the changes, so one weird year can't fool us.
definition.scientific: Median of all pairwise slopes; robust to outliers.

definition.simple: Counts how often later months are higher than earlier ones. If it happens far more than by chance, something is changing.
definition.scientific: Rank-based trend test; the Hamed–Rao variant corrects its variance for autocorrelation.

term.scientific: OLS t-test with effective sample size

definition.simple: Draws the best straight line through the data and checks if it really tilts, while remembering that months are not fully separate.
definition.scientific: Least-squares slope t-test with n_eff = n(1 − r₁)/(1 + r₁).

definition.simple: How many years of data we would need to be sure about a change this size.
definition.scientific: Weatherhead et al. (1998) estimate for 95% confidence and 90% power, given noise and autocorrelation.

definition.simple: Measured directly by an instrument, here a satellite.
definition.scientific: Retrieved from satellite measurements.

definition.simple: Worked out by a computer that mixes measurements with the laws of physics. Useful, but not a separate measurement.
definition.scientific: Model or reanalysis output; shares inputs with other products, so agreement is weaker evidence.

definition.simple: The satellite slowly started passing over later in the day, which can fake a change.
definition.scientific: Aqua stopped orbit maintenance in 2022; its equator-crossing time drifted later, biasing diurnal sampling.

definition.simple: The data comes as squares on a map. Bigger squares show less detail.
definition.scientific: One cell of the dataset's spatial grid (e.g. 1° × 1°).

definition.simple: If you check many things, a few will look changed just by luck. We correct for that.
definition.scientific: Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment of p-values across all variables scanned for a region (q = 0.05).

definition.simple: How full of water vapour the air is, from 0% (bone dry) to 100% (it can't hold more). Warmer air can hold more, so humidity drops when air warms up.
definition.scientific: Ratio of water-vapour pressure to saturation vapour pressure at the air temperature.

definition.simple: How much dust, smoke and pollution block sunlight.
definition.scientific: Vertically integrated aerosol extinction at 550 nm (unitless).

definition.simple: Sure it's real: two careful checks agree. Maybe: they don't agree yet. Too soon to tell: we need more years.
definition.scientific: Mapped from the verdict label: significant → sure; fragile or borderline → maybe; not significant → too soon.

definition.simple: We checked this measurement can answer the question here, before looking at the answer.
definition.scientific: Passes the stage-1 checks (question, fitness, detectability) before any trend is computed.

definition.simple: A computer mixed many measurements with the rules of physics to work this out. It is not a direct measurement.
definition.scientific: Model or reanalysis product (e.g. MERRA-2, GLDAS); not independent of the observations it assimilates.

definition.simple: How far a place is from the middle line of the Earth, going north or south.
definition.scientific: Angular distance north (+) or south (−) of the equator, in degrees.

definition.simple: How far a place is east or west of a line through London.
definition.scientific: Angular distance east (+) or west (−) of the prime meridian, in degrees.

definition.simple: A gas made when engines, power plants and factories burn fuel. A lot of it makes city air dirty.
definition.scientific: Tropospheric NO₂ vertical column density (molecules/cm²), a marker of combustion emissions; short-lived, so it stays near its sources.

definition.simple: A tool that measures. Some sit on satellites and look down at the Earth.
definition.scientific: A sensor on a satellite platform (e.g. AIRS on Aqua, OMI on Aura), or a computer model (MERRA-2, GLDAS), that produces a data product holding many variables.

definition.simple: One thing an instrument measures, like how warm the air is or how much rain falls.
definition.scientific: One measured quantity inside a data product (e.g. surface air temperature). It is what we test for a trend.

definition.simple: A machine that circles the Earth high up in space. It carries instruments.
definition.scientific: A spacecraft in orbit that carries one or more instruments (e.g. Aqua, Terra, Aura).

definition.simple: A computer program that works out past weather from many real measurements.
definition.scientific: A numerical model that assimilates many observations into gridded fields (e.g. MERRA-2, GLDAS). It is not itself a sensor.

definition.simple: We ask a second, different source about the same thing. If both say the same, we trust it more.
definition.scientific: The same quantity from an independent instrument or product over the shared years; direction is compared, not size.

definition.simple: Some satellites only see well on days without clouds. A month counts only if it has enough clear days.
definition.scientific: Daily products are averaged to months only when the month has at least the declared minimum number of valid days.
